\section{Introduction}\label{sec:intro}

For $C^*$-algebras $A,B\subseteq\B(H)$, write $A_1$ and $B_1$ for their
closed unit balls. Their Kadison--Kastler distance is
\begin{equation}\label{eq:kk}
\KK(A,B)=\max\left\{
\sup_{a\in A_1}\inf_{b\in B_1}\norm{a-b},\,
\sup_{b\in B_1}\inf_{a\in A_1}\norm{b-a}\right\}.
\end{equation}
The spatial form of the perturbation problem asks whether sufficiently close
algebras must be related by $uAu^*=B$ for a unitary $u\in\B(H)$.
Kadison and Kastler initiated this problem in \cite{KK72}. In its separable
$C^*$-algebraic form, one asks for a constant $\delta>0$ valid for all
norm-separable $C^*$-algebras on separable Hilbert spaces; no bound on
$\norm{u-\id}$ is required. The following theorem resolves negatively this
separable $C^*$-algebraic spatial form of the Kadison--Kastler conjecture,
even for unital algebras with a common identity.

\begin{theorem}\label{thm:main}
For every $\varepsilon>0$ there are a separable complex Hilbert space $H$
and unital, norm-separable $C^*$-algebras $A,B\subseteq\B(H)$ with common
identity $\id_H$ such that
\[
\KK(A,B)<\varepsilon,\qquad A''=B'',
\]
but no unitary $u\in\B(H)$ satisfies $uAu^*=B$.
\end{theorem}

The scope of this statement is important. Johnson constructed arbitrarily
close separable nuclear algebras for which implementing unitaries cannot be
chosen close to the identity \cite{Johnson82}; those examples are nevertheless
spatially conjugate. Choi and Christensen constructed arbitrarily close
nonisomorphic algebras \cite{CC83}, but norm nonseparability is essential to
those examples. These distinctions, and the resulting separable spatial
formulation, are discussed in \cite{CSSWW10}. In the positive direction,
Christensen, Sinclair, Smith, White, and Winter proved spatial conjugacy for
sufficiently close separable nuclear $C^*$-algebras on a separable Hilbert
space \cite[Theorem~4]{CSSWW10}; see \cite[Theorem~5.4]{CSSWW12} for the full
proof. Theorem~\ref{thm:main} imposes no nuclearity
assumption. It makes no assertion of abstract nonisomorphism and does not
give a counterexample for von Neumann algebras.

\paragraph{The construction.}
We first isolate a way to turn an obstruction for inclusions into an
obstruction to arbitrary spatial conjugacy. Let $D\subseteq\B(L)$ be unital,
norm-separable, and have scalar center. For unital subalgebras $P,Q\subseteq D$,
consider the algebra
\[
\E_D(P)=\{(x_n):x_n\in D,\ x_n\longrightarrow p\in P
\text{ in norm}\}
\]
acting diagonally on $\bigoplus_{n\ge1}L$. Changing $P$ changes only the
condition at the limit. The coordinate projections are intrinsic minimal
central projections of this algebra. Consequently, a unitary conjugating
$\E_D(P)$ onto $\E_D(Q)$ must permute the coordinates and normalize $D$
on every coordinate. Pulling back constant sequences then forces each
finite family in $Q$ to be a simultaneous norm limit of families in
unitary conjugates of $P$ by normalizers of $D$.

Write $D'$ for the commutant of $D$ on $L$, consisting of the bounded
operators commuting with every element of $D$. The obstruction we use is
the equality
\begin{equation}\label{eq:intro-test}
\norm{\sum_i p_i z_i}_{\B(L)}
=\norm{\sum_i p_i\otimes z_i}_{\B(L\otimes L)},
\qquad p_i\in P,\quad z_i\in D'.
\end{equation}
This equality is invariant under normalizers of $D$ and passes to
simultaneous finite-family norm limits. We construct very close subalgebras
$P_0,P_t\subseteq D$ for which it holds for $P_0$ but fails for $P_t$.
In fact, $P_0$ and $P_t$ themselves are conjugate by a unitary close to the
identity. The obstruction concerns their positions inside $D$, and the
sequence construction makes it an obstruction to every spatial conjugacy
of the resulting algebras.

For the close inclusions we use a real-parameter deformation of the regular
representation of the free group on countably many generators. This
representation-theoretic ingredient belongs to the Pytlik--Szwarc family
\cite{PS86}; its uniform-topology behavior at the regular representation
is discussed by Burger, Ozawa, and Thom \cite[Theorem~4.6]{BOT13}.
We give a direct tree construction and prove the uniform estimate needed
here. The additional mechanism is the combination of the relative
tensor-norm test with the convergent-sequence reduction. The reduction is
stated separately, so it can be used for other pairs of inclusions.

Section~\ref{sec:sequences} proves the reduction.
Section~\ref{sec:tree} constructs the representations, and
Section~\ref{sec:inclusions} establishes the tensor-norm obstruction.
Section~\ref{sec:assembly} assembles the counterexamples.
All Hilbert spaces are complex, and all operator tensor products below act
on the indicated Hilbert-space tensor products. No abstract choice of
$C^*$-tensor norm is needed. Unital subalgebras are understood to contain
the identity of their ambient operator algebra.

\section{A convergent-sequence obstruction}\label{sec:sequences}

We explain how the limit condition records an inclusion $P\subseteq D$.
The resulting algebras preserve the distance between limit algebras, but
their spatial conjugacies are constrained by the coordinate algebra $D$.

\begin{proposition}\label{prop:sequences}
Let $L$ be a nonzero separable Hilbert space, let $D\subseteq\B(L)$ be a
unital norm-separable $C^*$-algebra with $Z(D)=\C\id_L$, and let
$P,Q\subseteq D$ be unital $C^*$-subalgebras containing $\id_L$.
On $H=\bigoplus_{n\ge1}L$, define
\begin{equation}\label{eq:sequence-definition}
\E_D(P)=\{(x_n)_{n\ge1}:x_n\in D,\ x_n\to p\in P\text{ in norm}\},
\end{equation}
and define $\E_D(Q)$ similarly. Then:
\begin{enumerate}
\item These are unital norm-separable $C^*$-algebras with common identity,
and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:distance-equality}
\KK(\E_D(P),\E_D(Q))=\KK(P,Q).
\end{equation}
\item If a unitary conjugates $\E_D(P)$ onto $\E_D(Q)$, there are unitaries
$U_n\in\B(L)$ with $U_nDU_n^*=D$ such that, for every $b\in Q$, some
$p_b\in P$ satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{eq:pointwise-normalizers}
\norm{b-U_np_bU_n^*}\longrightarrow0.
\end{equation}
The same sequence $(U_n)$ works for every $b$.
\item The two algebras have the same commutant, and hence the same
von Neumann closure.
\end{enumerate}
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
A norm-convergent sequence is bounded, so \eqref{eq:sequence-definition}
defines a diagonal operator on $H$, with norm $\sup_n\norm{x_n}$.
Algebra operations and adjoints preserve the limit condition, and the
constant identity belongs to the algebra. To check norm closedness,
suppose $x^{(k)}\to x$ in the supremum norm, with coordinate limits
$p_k\in P$. Then
\[
\norm{p_k-p_j}\le\sup_n\norm{x_n^{(k)}-x_n^{(j)}}.
\]
Thus $p_k\to p\in P$. The estimate
\[
\norm{x_n-p}\le\norm{x_n-x_n^{(k)}}
+\norm{x_n^{(k)}-p_k}+\norm{p_k-p}
\]
shows that $x_n\to p$. Moreover,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:sum-decomposition}
\E_D(P)=c_0(\N,D)+\{(p,p,\ldots):p\in P\}.
\end{equation}
The two summands are norm-separable: $P$ is a subspace of the separable
metric space $D$, and finite-support sequences from a countable dense
subset of $D$ are dense in $c_0(\N,D)$. Their sum is norm-separable.

For the metric assertion, write
$\alpha(P,Q)=\sup_{p\in P_1}\dist(p,Q_1)$.
Given a contraction $x\in\E_D(P)$ with limit $p$ and $\eta>0$, choose
$q\in Q_1$ with $\norm{p-q}<\alpha(P,Q)+\eta$, and choose $N$ so that
$\sup_{n>N}\norm{x_n-p}<\eta$. Keeping the first $N$ entries of $x$ and
putting $q$ thereafter gives a contraction $y\in\E_D(Q)$ with
$\norm{x-y}<\alpha(P,Q)+2\eta$. This proves the upper bound for the
directed distance. Conversely, for a constant contraction $(p,p,\ldots)$
and any contraction $y\in\E_D(Q)$ with limit $q\in Q_1$,
\[
\norm{(p,p,\ldots)-y}=\sup_n\norm{p-y_n}\ge\norm{p-q}
\ge\dist(p,Q_1).
\]
Taking infima and suprema proves equality of the directed distances.
Interchanging $P,Q$ gives \eqref{eq:distance-equality}.

Let $e_n$ be the projection onto the $n$th copy of $L$. Every $e_n$ is a
central element of $\E_D(P)$. Conversely, a central element $(x_n)$
commutes with all finite-support $D$-valued sequences, so each $x_n$ lies
in $Z(D)=\C\id_L$. Thus the center consists exactly of convergent scalar
sequences. Every nonzero central projection contains an $e_n$, and hence
the minimal nonzero central projections are precisely the $e_n$.
The same holds for $\E_D(Q)$.

If $S\E_D(P)S^*=\E_D(Q)$, conjugation by $S$ therefore permutes the
projections $e_n$. Its restriction from the $n$th coordinate to its image
is a unitary $U_n:L\to L$. The corresponding coordinate corners of both
algebras are exactly $D$, since every finitely supported $D$-valued
sequence is allowed. Consequently $U_nDU_n^*=D$. For $b\in Q$, pull back
the constant sequence $(b,b,\ldots)$ under $S$. Its $n$th entry is
$U_n^*bU_n$, regardless of the coordinate permutation. It belongs to
$\E_D(P)$, so its entries converge in norm to some $p_b\in P$.
This is equivalent to \eqref{eq:pointwise-normalizers} and proves (ii).

Finally, an operator commuting with $\E_D(P)$ commutes with all $e_n$,
so it is block diagonal. Commutation with the finite-support $D$ corners
means that each block lies in $D'$. These conditions are also sufficient,
and do not depend on $P$. Thus both commutants equal
\[
\{(z_n):z_n\in D',\ \sup_n\norm{z_n}<\infty\}.
\]
This proves (iii).
\end{proof}

We next give a concrete condition preserved by the
approximation in Proposition~\ref{prop:sequences}(ii).

\begin{definition}\label{def:tensor}
For a unital inclusion $P\subseteq D\subseteq\B(L)$, say that $P$ has
the \emph{spatial tensor-norm identity relative to $D$} if
\begin{equation}\label{eq:tensor-property}
\norm{\sum_{i=1}^m p_i z_i}_{\B(L)}
=\norm{\sum_{i=1}^m p_i\otimes z_i}_{\B(L\otimes L)}
\end{equation}
for every positive integer $m$, all $p_1,\ldots,p_m\in P$, and all
$z_1,\ldots,z_m\in D'$.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:invariant}
Let $P,Q\subseteq D\subseteq\B(L)$ be unital $C^*$-algebras.
The identity in Definition~\ref{def:tensor} is preserved by conjugating
$P$ with any unitary normalizing $D$. If $(U_n)$ is a sequence of unitaries
in $\B(L)$ satisfying $U_nDU_n^*=D$ and every $b\in Q$ admits the
approximation \eqref{eq:pointwise-normalizers}, then the identity for $P$
implies the identity for $Q$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
If $UDU^*=D$, then $UD'U^*=D'$. For $q_i=Up_iU^*$ and $z_i\in D'$,
apply \eqref{eq:tensor-property} to $p_i$ and $U^*z_iU$. Conjugate its
product sum by $U$ and its tensor sum by $U\otimes U$. This gives
\eqref{eq:tensor-property} for $q_i,z_i$.

Now fix finite families $b_i\in Q$ and $z_i\in D'$. Put
$q_{i,n}=U_np_{b_i}U_n^*$. For each $n$, the first part gives the identity
for the entire list $(q_{i,n})_i$, since its entries all lie in
$U_nPU_n^*$. Both errors
\[
\norm{\sum_i(q_{i,n}-b_i)z_i},\qquad
\norm{\sum_i(q_{i,n}-b_i)\otimes z_i}
\]
are at most $\sum_i\norm{q_{i,n}-b_i}\norm{z_i}$, which tends to zero.
Taking the limit proves the identity for the prescribed families in
$Q$ and $D'$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}\label{cor:obstruction}
Under the hypotheses of Proposition~\ref{prop:sequences}, suppose that
$P$ has the spatial tensor-norm identity relative to $D$, whereas $Q$
does not. Then $\E_D(P)$ and $\E_D(Q)$ are not spatially conjugate.
If $W\in\B(L)$ is unitary and $WPW^*=Q$, then nevertheless
\[
\KK(\E_D(P),\E_D(Q))\le2\norm{W-\id_L}.
\]
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
A spatial conjugacy would give the unitaries in
Proposition~\ref{prop:sequences}(ii), contradicting
Lemma~\ref{lem:invariant}. For the distance bound,
$p\mapsto WpW^*$ bijects the closed unit balls and
\[
\norm{WpW^*-p}\le2\norm{p}\norm{W-\id_L}.
\]
Apply Proposition~\ref{prop:sequences}(i).
\end{proof}

The unitary $W$ used for the distance estimate is not required to normalize $D$.
Indeed, under the stated tensor-norm obstruction, no unitary normalizing
$D$ can conjugate $P$ onto $Q$.

\begin{lemma}[Absorption]\label{lem:absorption}
Let $\sigma$ be a unitary representation of $G$ on a nonzero Hilbert space
$J$. The operator
\[
W_\sigma(\delta_x\otimes v)=\delta_x\otimes\sigma(x)v
\quad(x\in G,\ v\in J)
\]
is unitary on $K\otimes J$ and satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{eq:absorption}
W_\sigma(\lambda(g)\otimes\id_J)W_\sigma^*
=\lambda(g)\otimes\sigma(g)\quad(g\in G).
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The operator is the orthogonal direct sum of the unitaries $\sigma(x)$.
On $\delta_x\otimes v$, the left side of \eqref{eq:absorption} equals
\[
\delta_{gx}\otimes\sigma(gx)\sigma(x)^*v
=\delta_{gx}\otimes\sigma(g)v.
\qedhere
\]
\end{proof}

\qquad \id_K\otimes E_{xy}\quad(x,y\in G).
\end{equation}
The generators include the identity, and $P_0,P_t\subseteq D$.
All three algebras are norm-separable, since their generating sets are
countable.

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:ambient}
The algebra $D$ in \eqref{eq:D} has scalar center, and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:commutant}
D'=\{Y\otimes\id_K:Y\in\lambda(G)'\}.
\end{equation}
There is a unitary $W\in\B(L)$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:close-W}
WP_0W^*=P_t,\qquad \norm{W-\id_L}\le c(t).
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Commutation with all $\id_K\otimes E_{xy}$ forces a bounded operator to
be $Y\otimes\id_K$: commutation with the diagonal matrix units removes
off-diagonal blocks, and commutation with the remaining units makes the
diagonal blocks identical. The first-factor generators then impose
exactly $Y\in\lambda(G)'$. Such operators commute with all the
second-factor generators, proving \eqref{eq:commutant}. In particular,
$\rho(g)\otimes\id_K\in D'$.

If $Y\otimes\id_K\in Z(D)$, then $Y$ commutes with $\lambda(G)$ by
\eqref{eq:commutant}. It also commutes with $\rho(G)$, since
$Y\otimes\id_K$ belongs to $D$ and the right translations belong to
$D'$. Thus $Y\delta_e$ is invariant under $\lambda(g)\rho(g)$, which
acts on the basis by conjugation $x\mapsto gxg^{-1}$.
Every nonidentity conjugacy class in $G$ is infinite: conjugate a fixed
nonidentity reduced word by distinct generators absent from that word.
A square-summable vector invariant under conjugation must therefore be
supported at $e$. Write $Y\delta_e=\alpha\delta_e$. Commuting with left
translations gives $Y\delta_x=\alpha\delta_x$ for every $x$, proving
$Z(D)=\C\id_L$.

For the final assertion, Lemma~\ref{lem:absorption} shows that
$W=W_{\pi_t}W_{\pi_0}^*$ sends every $Q_0(g)$ to $Q_t(g)$ by conjugation.
Moreover, the direct-sum description of these unitaries gives
\[
\norm{W-\id_L}=\norm{W_{\pi_t}-W_{\pi_0}}
=\sup_{x\in G}\norm{\pi_t(x)-\lambda(x)}\le c(t).
\qedhere
\]
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:good-inclusion}
The inclusion $P_0\subseteq D$ has the spatial tensor-norm identity.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Define a unitary on $L$ by
\[
V(v\otimes\delta_x)=\lambda(x)^*v\otimes\delta_x.
\]
It commutes with every element of $D'$ by \eqref{eq:commutant}.
On elementary vectors one computes
\[
VQ_0(g)V^*(v\otimes\delta_x)=v\otimes\delta_{gx}.
\]
Thus $VP_0V^*=\id_K\otimes C^*(\lambda(G))$.
Given finite families $p_i\in P_0$ and $z_i\in D'$, write
\[
Vp_iV^*=\id_K\otimes X_i,\qquad z_i=Y_i\otimes\id_K.
\]
Conjugation by $V$ gives
\[
\norm{\sum_i p_i z_i}=\norm{\sum_i Y_i\otimes X_i}.
\]
On $L\otimes L=K^{\otimes4}$, conjugation by $V\otimes\id_L$ gives
\[
\norm{\sum_i p_i\otimes z_i}
=\norm{\sum_i\id_K\otimes X_i\otimes Y_i\otimes\id_K}
=\norm{\sum_iY_i\otimes X_i}.
\]
The last equality permutes the four tensor factors and uses the fact
that tensoring with a nonzero identity operator does not change norm.
This proves \eqref{eq:tensor-property}.
\end{proof}

For $P_t$, the identity will fail because the product norm has a lower
bound linear in the number of generators, while absorption gives a
square-root upper bound on the tensor norm.

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:free-norm}
For every positive integer $m$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:free-norm}
\norm{\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda(s_i)}\le2\sqrt m.
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Let $F_i$ be the orthogonal projection onto the closed span of words beginning
with $s_i^{-1}$. The $F_i$ are pairwise orthogonal. Write
$\lambda(s_i)=A_i+B_i$, where
\[
A_i=\lambda(s_i)(\id_K-F_i),\qquad B_i=\lambda(s_i)F_i.
\]
There is no cancellation when $s_i$ is prepended to a word not beginning
with $s_i^{-1}$. Thus the range of $A_i$ consists of vectors supported on
words beginning with $s_i$, and these ranges are mutually orthogonal.
For every $v\in K$,
\[
\norm{\sum_i A_iv}^2=\sum_i\norm{(\id_K-F_i)v}^2
\le m\norm{v}^2,
\]
while
\[
\norm{\sum_i B_iv}\le\sum_i\norm{F_iv}
\le\sqrt m\left(\sum_i\norm{F_iv}^2\right)^{1/2}
\le\sqrt m\norm{v}.
\]
Adding the two bounds proves \eqref{eq:free-norm}.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:bad-inclusion}
For every $0<t<1$, the inclusion $P_t\subseteq D$
fails the spatial tensor-norm identity.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Choose an integer $m>4/t^2$, so $mt>2\sqrt m$, and take
\[
p_i=Q_t(s_i),\qquad z_i=\rho(s_i)\otimes\id_K,
\qquad 1\le i\le m.
\]
These belong to $P_t$ and $D'$, respectively. Since
$\lambda(s_i)\rho(s_i)\delta_e=\delta_e$, \eqref{eq:coefficient} implies
\begin{equation}\label{eq:large-norm}
\norm{\sum_i p_i z_i}
\ge\left|\inner{\left(\sum_i p_i z_i\right)
(\delta_e\otimes\delta_e)}{\delta_e\otimes\delta_e}\right|
=mt.
\end{equation}
On the other hand, the tensor sum on $L\otimes L$ is
\[
\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda(s_i)\otimes\pi_t(s_i)
\otimes\rho(s_i)\otimes\id_K.
\]
Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:absorption} to the representation
$\sigma=\pi_t\otimes\rho\otimes1$ on $K^{\otimes3}$, where $1$ is the
trivial representation on the last copy of $K$. Together with
Lemma~\ref{lem:free-norm}, it gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:small-norm}
\norm{\sum_i p_i\otimes z_i}
=\norm{\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda(s_i)}\le2\sqrt m<mt.
\end{equation}
Equations~\eqref{eq:large-norm} and \eqref{eq:small-norm} contradict the
identity for this finite list.
\end{proof}

\section{The counterexamples}\label{sec:assembly}

\begin{proof}[Proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:main}]
Given $\varepsilon>0$, choose $0<t<1$ so small that $2c(t)<\varepsilon$.
Use the algebras $P_0,P_t\subseteq D\subseteq\B(L)$ from
Section~\ref{sec:inclusions}, and put
\[
H=\bigoplus_{n\ge1}L,\qquad A=\E_D(P_0),\qquad B=\E_D(P_t).
\]
The space $H$ is separable. Lemma~\ref{lem:ambient} supplies the scalar
center of $D$, so Proposition~\ref{prop:sequences} shows that $A,B$ are
unital norm-separable $C^*$-algebras with common identity and that
$A''=B''$. The same lemma supplies a unitary $W$ with
$WP_0W^*=P_t$ and $\norm{W-\id_L}\le c(t)$. By
Corollary~\ref{cor:obstruction},
\[
\KK(A,B)\le2c(t)<\varepsilon.
\]
Finally, Lemmas~\ref{lem:good-inclusion} and~\ref{lem:bad-inclusion}
show that the relative tensor-norm identity holds for $P_0$ but not for
$P_t$. Corollary~\ref{cor:obstruction} therefore excludes every unitary
conjugating $A$ onto $B$.
\end{proof}

The common ideal $c_0(\N,D)$ makes the von Neumann closures agree,
while the norm-limit condition retains the distinction between the two
inclusions.

\section{Introduction}\label{sec:introduction}

Let $M$ and $N$ be von Neumann algebras acting on a complex Hilbert
space $H$, both with identity $I_H$.  Their one-sided near-inclusion gap is
\begin{equation}\label{eq:gamma-definition}
 \gamma(M,N)=\sup_{\substack{x\in M\\\|x\|\leq 1}}
                   \inf_{y\in N}\|x-y\|.
\end{equation}
The approximating element $y$ is not required to be contractive.  A small
value of $\gamma(M,N)$ says that every contraction in $M$ is close to some
element of $N$; it does not require these choices of approximants to
preserve algebraic operations.  If a unitary $u$ satisfies $uMu^*\subseteq N$,
then $\gamma(M,N)\leq 2\|u-I_H\|$.  The converse question asks whether a
small near inclusion can always be obtained in this way.

The underlying perturbation program began with Kadison and Kastler
\cite{KK1972}.  They measured the distance between operator algebras by
the Hausdorff distance between their unit balls in the operator norm,
now called the Kadison--Kastler distance, and proposed that sufficiently
close von Neumann algebras should be related by a unitary close to the
identity.  Christensen, Johnson, and Raeburn--Taylor established the
amenable case in the 1970s
\cite{Chr1977,Joh1977,RT1977}.  Christensen subsequently introduced
near inclusions and proved a spatial embedding theorem for an amenable
source algebra and an arbitrary target
\cite[Definition~2.1 and Theorem~4.3]{Chr1980}.  In particular, sufficiently
small near inclusions in this setting admit implementing unitaries whose
distance from the identity is bounded linearly by the near-inclusion
tolerance.

We use the following formulation of the unrestricted one-sided question
posed by Cameron, Christensen, Sinclair, Smith, White, and Wiggins in
the paragraph preceding \cite[Theorem~2]{CCSSWW2012}:
\begin{quote}
For every $\varepsilon>0$, is there a $\delta>0$ such that, for every
complex Hilbert space $H$ and every pair of von Neumann algebras
$M,N\subseteq\mathcal B(H)$ with common identity $I_H$,
$\gamma(M,N)<\delta$ implies the existence of a unitary
$u\in\mathcal B(H)$ satisfying
\[
 uMu^*\subseteq N
 \qquad\text{and}\qquad
 \|u-I_H\|<\varepsilon?
\]
\end{quote}
Here $\delta$ must be independent of the algebras and their
representations.  We answer this question negatively.

\begin{theorem}\label{thm:main}
There exist $\varepsilon_0>0$, separable complex Hilbert spaces $H_n$,
and von Neumann algebras $M_n,N_n\subseteq\mathcal B(H_n)$ with common
identity $I_{H_n}$ such that
\[
 \gamma(M_n,N_n)\longrightarrow 0,
\]
but, for all sufficiently large $n$, every unitary
$u\in\mathcal B(H_n)$ satisfying $uM_nu^*\subseteq N_n$ obeys
\[
 \|u-I_{H_n}\|\geq\varepsilon_0.
\]
\end{theorem}

In these examples a unitary embedding of $M_n$ into $N_n$ does exist;
the obstruction concerns its distance from the identity.  The theorem
therefore separates normwise approximation from small spatial
implementation even on separable Hilbert spaces.  Its hypothesis is
one-sided.  The construction supplies no reverse near inclusion, and
hence does not give a counterexample to the two-sided Kadison--Kastler
conjecture.  The positive results for nonamenable factors in
\cite{CCSSWW2012}, which concern two-sided perturbations under additional
structural hypotheses, address a different assertion.

The proof transfers a classical finite-dimensional obstruction into the
near-inclusion problem.  Voiculescu's clock and shift matrices
$U_n,V_n\in\mathcal B(\mathbb C^n)$ satisfy
$\|U_nV_n-V_nU_n\|\to0$, but cannot be approximated in norm by commuting
unitary pairs \cite{Voi1983}.  Exel and Loring gave an elementary
winding-number proof of this phenomenon \cite{EL1989}; we use its trace-logarithm form
\cite[Lemma~3.1]{Exel1993}.  We recall the short obstruction argument
in Section~\ref{sec:obstruction}.

To place these matrices in operator algebras, we use the free group
$\F$ on countably many generators.  The starting representation
is the real-parameter Pytlik--Szwarc representation
\cite[\S2.3, Equation~(5)]{PS1986}, whose cyclic coefficient is Haagerup's
positive-definite function $g\mapsto t^{|g|}$, $0<t<1$, where $|g|$ is
reduced word length \cite[Lemma~1.2]{Haa1979}.
Section~\ref{sec:circle} gives a self-contained
tree realization at $t=1/2$ and adds a circle parameter $z$.
The norms of its Fourier coefficients are bounded, uniformly over the
group, by a sequence with summable first moment.  Along successive
distinct free generators, the values of the representations converge
in the weak operator topology to $tz$ times the projection onto the
identity vector in $\ell^2(\F)$.  Substituting $U_n$ and $V_n$ for the
circle parameter therefore produces two unitary representations of
$\F$ whose weak limits retain the original matrices.

Two further steps connect this representation family to the theorem.
In Section~\ref{sec:near}, a diagonal unitary built from the two
representations conjugates a copy of the group von Neumann algebra of
$\F\times\F$.  The target $N_n$ is the commutant of an amplified right
regular representation of this product group.  Reordering the Fourier
expansions gives an approximant in $N_n$ and an error bounded by a
constant times $\|U_nV_n-V_nU_n\|$.  Crucially, this estimate holds on the
entire unit ball of the source algebra.  In
Section~\ref{sec:obstruction}, a hypothetical sequence of spatial
embeddings tending to the identity places the conjugated left regular
representation in $N_n$, where it commutes with the right regular
representation.  Their pointwise product is then a representation of
$\F\times\F$, so the von Neumann algebras generated by its two factors
commute.  Weak operator
limits in these algebras recover operators close to copies of
$U_n$ and $V_n$ supported on projections.  Perturbing those projections,
compressing to a common finite-dimensional corner, and taking polar
parts would yield
commuting unitary matrices close to $U_n,V_n$, contradicting the
winding-number obstruction.

\section{A circle family with uniform Fourier bounds}\label{sec:circle}

We first construct representations in which a scalar circle parameter can
later be replaced by a unitary matrix. Two properties are needed: Fourier
coefficients with a summable first moment, uniformly over the group, and
a weak operator limit that retains the parameter.

Let $F$ be the free group on generators $s_j$, $j\geq 1$, with identity
$e$. Put $K=\ell^2(F)$, write $(\delta_x)_{x\in F}$ for its standard
orthonormal basis, and let $p_e$ be the projection onto
$\mathbb C\delta_e$. We use the left regular representation
$l(g)\delta_x=\delta_{gx}$. Throughout the construction,
\[
 t=\frac12,\qquad r=(1-t^2)^{1/2},\qquad
 \mathbb T=\{z\in\mathbb C:|z|=1\}.
\]

\begin{proposition}\label{prop:circle}
There are unitary representations $\pi_z:F\to\B(K)$, indexed by
$z\in\mathbb T$, and operators $A_k(g)\in\B(K)$, indexed by
$k\in\mathbb Z$ and $g\in F$, such that
\begin{align}
 \pi_z(g)&=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}z^kA_k(g),
 &\sup_{g\in F}\|A_k(g)\|&\leq c_k,
 &c_k&=\mathbf 1_{\{k=0\}}+\frac{2t^{|k|}}{1-t},
 \label{eq:fourier}\\
 \pi_z(s_j)&\xrightarrow[j\to\infty]{\WOT}tzp_e.
 \label{eq:circle-limit}
\end{align}
The series in \eqref{eq:fourier} converges absolutely in operator norm,
uniformly in $g$ and $z$, and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:moments}
 S_0:=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}c_k<\infty,
 \qquad S_1:=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}|k|c_k<\infty.
\end{equation}
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
The underlying representation is the real-parameter Pytlik--Szwarc
representation \cite[Section~2.3, Equation~(5)]{PS1986}; its cyclic
coefficient is the positive-definite function $g\mapsto t^{|g|}$
of Haagerup \cite[Lemma~1.2]{Haa1979}. We give the tree construction
before introducing the circle parameter.

Use the Cayley tree whose edges join $x$ to $xs_j^{\pm1}$, rooted at
$e$, and write $p(x)$ for the parent of $x\ne e$. Define
\begin{equation}\label{eq:tree-vectors}
 \xi_e=\delta_e,\qquad
 \xi_x=t\xi_{p(x)}+r\delta_x\quad(x\ne e).
\end{equation}
All these vectors have norm one. If $v$ is the last common vertex of the
paths from $e$ to $x$ and $y$, the two tails beyond $v$ are orthogonal
to each other and to $\xi_v$. Thus
\[
 \langle\xi_x,\xi_y\rangle
 =t^{d(x,v)+d(y,v)}=t^{d(x,y)},
\]
where $d$ is the tree distance. Their linear span contains every
$\delta_x$, by \eqref{eq:tree-vectors}. Left multiplication preserves
$d$, so the rule
\[
 \pi(g)\xi_x=\xi_{gx}
\]
extends to a unitary on $K$. These unitaries form a representation.

The difference from the regular representation is confined to a single
finite path. To see this precisely, put $T_g=\pi(g)l(g)^*$.
For $y\ne g$, \eqref{eq:tree-vectors} gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:root-change}
 T_g\delta_y=
 \frac{\xi_y-t\xi_{g p(g^{-1}y)}}{r},
 \qquad T_g\delta_g=\xi_g.
\end{equation}
The vertex $g p(g^{-1}y)$ is the first step from $y$ toward $g$.
Let $e=h_0,h_1,\ldots,h_d=g$ be the path from $e$ to $g$.
For $y$ outside this path, the first steps toward $e$ and $g$
coincide; hence $T_g\delta_y=\delta_y$. On the path,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:path-action}
 T_g\delta_{h_b}=r\xi_{h_b}-t\delta_{h_{b+1}}\quad(0\leq b<d),
 \qquad T_g\delta_{h_d}=\xi_{h_d}.
\end{equation}
In particular, the path subspace and its orthogonal complement reduce
$T_g$. Expanding the vectors along the path gives
\[
 \xi_{h_b}=t^b\delta_{h_0}
       +r\sum_{a=1}^b t^{b-a}\delta_{h_a}.
\]
By \eqref{eq:path-action}, the subdiagonal entries are $-t$; every
other nonzero entry in row $a$, column $b$ is $t^{|a-b|}$ times
$1$, $r$, or $r^2$. Thus the matrix entries on this subspace satisfy
\begin{equation}\label{eq:path-decay}
 |(T_g)_{a,b}|\leq t^{|a-b|}\qquad(0\leq a,b\leq d).
\end{equation}
This also includes $g=e$, when $T_e=I$.

Let $q:F\to\mathbb Z$ be the homomorphism with $q(s_j)=1$ for every
$j$, and define $D_z\delta_x=z^{-q(x)}\delta_x$. The desired
representation is
\begin{equation}\label{eq:circle-twist}
 \pi_z(g)=z^{q(g)}D_z\pi(g)D_z^*
          =(D_zT_gD_z^*)l(g).
\end{equation}
The first expression proves that it is a unitary representation. The
second follows from $D_zl(g)D_z^*=z^{-q(g)}l(g)$ and supplies its
Fourier bounds.

On the path subspace, the entry in row $a$, column $b$ acquires the
Laurent factor $z^{q(h_b)-q(h_a)}$. Each edge changes $q$ by $1$ or
$-1$, so an entry of exponent $k$ can occur only when $|a-b|\geq|k|$.
For each row or column there are at most two entries at any given
distance $m$. By \eqref{eq:path-decay}, the absolute row and column
sums of the coefficient of $z^k$ are therefore at most
\[
 2\sum_{m\geq|k|}t^m=\frac{2t^{|k|}}{1-t}.
\]
Outside the path the operator is the identity, which contributes only
to the coefficient at $k=0$. The row and column sum bound for operator
norm, followed by multiplication by $l(g)$, proves
\eqref{eq:fourier}. For each fixed $g$ this is a finite Laurent
expansion; the common bounds $c_k$ give the asserted uniform absolute
convergence and \eqref{eq:moments}.

Finally, \eqref{eq:path-action} and \eqref{eq:circle-twist} give
\[
 \pi_z(s_j)\delta_e=tz\delta_e+r\delta_{s_j}.
\]
For any fixed $x\ne e$, all sufficiently large $j$ satisfy
$s_jx\notin\{e,s_j\}$, and then
$\pi_z(s_j)\delta_x=\delta_{s_jx}$. These basis-vector calculations,
together with the uniform norm bound $\|\pi_z(s_j)\|=1$, prove
\eqref{eq:circle-limit}.
\end{proof}

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

For a von Neumann algebra $M\subseteq\B(H)$, write $M_1$ for its
closed operator-norm unit ball. The Kadison--Kastler distance between
two such algebras is
\begin{equation}\label{eq:kk-definition}
 d(M,N)=\max\left\{
 \sup_{x\in M_1}\inf_{y\in N_1}\norm{x-y},\quad
 \sup_{y\in N_1}\inf_{x\in M_1}\norm{x-y}\right\}.
\end{equation}
Kadison and Kastler introduced this metric in 1972
\cite{KadisonKastler1972}. Their perturbation problem asks whether
closeness of the unit balls forces spatial isomorphism, implemented by
a unitary close to the identity. We prove the uniform form of this
assertion.

\begin{theorem}[Strong Kadison--Kastler stability]\label{thm:main}
For every $\eps>0$ there is $\delta=\delta(\eps)>0$ such that the
following holds. If $H$ is any complex Hilbert space and
$M,N\subseteq\B(H)$ are unital von Neumann algebras with identity
$I_H$ and $d(M,N)<\delta$, there is a unitary $u\in\B(H)$ satisfying
\[
 uMu^*=N,\qquad \norm{u-I_H}<\eps.
\]
\end{theorem}

The tolerance is independent of the algebras, their type, their
representations, and the cardinalities of their preduals and Hilbert
spaces. Thus \Cref{thm:main} resolves the strong Kadison--Kastler
conjecture positively. Its hypothesis concerns the ordinary distance
\eqref{eq:kk-definition}.

\subsection{Historical context}

Early positive results treated type~I algebras:
Phillips proved spatial isomorphism, and Christensen obtained a conjugating
unitary close to the identity \cite{Phillips1974,Christensen1975}.
The work of Christensen, Johnson, and Raeburn--Taylor established the
amenable case \cite{Christensen1977,Johnson1977,RaeburnTaylor1977}.
Christensen subsequently developed the one-sided theory of near inclusions:
an amenable von Neumann algebra sufficiently nearly contained in another
can be moved into it by a small unitary \cite{Christensen1980}.
His earlier work also treated close von Neumann subalgebras of a common
finite von Neumann algebra \cite{Christensen1977II}. The common finite
ambient algebra is an essential hypothesis of that result; merely assuming
that both represented algebras are finite gives a different problem.
In a different common-ambient setting, Ino proved near-identity unitary
conjugacy for sufficiently close subalgebras of a countably decomposable
ambient algebra when both admit conditional expectations of finite
probabilistic index from that algebra \cite[Theorem~3.2]{Ino2016}.

The corresponding development for $C^*$-algebras clarifies the role of the
conclusion. Christensen, Sinclair, Smith, White, and Winter proved that
sufficiently close $C^*$-algebras acting on a separable Hilbert space
are spatially isomorphic if one of them is norm separable and nuclear
\cite{CSSWW2010,CSSWW2012}.
Johnson's examples exclude a uniform bound on the displacement of an
implementing unitary that tends to zero with the algebra distance;
they do not exclude spatial isomorphism \cite{Johnson1982}.

For nonamenable von Neumann algebras, Cameron, Christensen, Sinclair, Smith,
White, and Wiggins constructed strongly stable factors of the form
$(L^\infty(X)\rtimes\mathrm{SL}_n(\mathbb Z))\barotimes R$, where
$n\geq3$, the action is free, ergodic, and probability preserving on a
standard nonatomic probability space, and $R$ is the hyperfinite
type~$\mathrm{II}_1$ factor \cite{CCSSWW2012,CCSSWW2014}.
Their proof combines amenable near-inclusion methods, a common standard
representation, and bounded cohomology. Their later work transfers
property~$\Gamma$ and Cartan structure between sufficiently close type
$\II_1$ factors with separable predual, and also studies stability of
solidity, strong solidity, and tensor-product structure
\cite{CCSSWW2017}.

The passage between representations is tied to Kadison's similarity
problem: whether a bounded homomorphism from a $C^*$-algebra into
$\B(H)$ is conjugate by an invertible operator to a $*$-homomorphism.
Christensen's work on property~$\Gamma$ factors provides a
foundational special case \cite{Christensen1986,Christensen2001}.
Christensen, Sinclair, Smith, and White established perturbation results
for the similarity property and operator-algebraic invariants
\cite{CSSW2010}; Cameron and collaborators then proved that the similarity
property is equivalent to continuity of commutants, with the required
uniformity over representations \cite{CCSSWW2013}.
These results explain why ordinary norm closeness, control at all matrix
levels, and implementation on the original Hilbert space must be kept
distinct throughout a proof of strong stability.
The companion manuscript \cite{OpenAI2026Similarity} also proves a
uniform commutator estimate, using invariant tensors and a free-corner
Hankel test. The amplification argument here instead uses free-word
randomization and is proved independently. Neither commutator estimate
alone constructs a nearby multiplicative correspondence between two
algebras; Appendix~\ref{app:comparison} compares their scope and this
remaining perturbation step.

The unit-ball metric supplies nearby elements but does not specify a
linear or multiplicative correspondence. We must construct such a
correspondence and control its implementation on the given Hilbert space,
with estimates independent of the algebras and representations.

We use normalized traces on finite factors and the standard comparison
and subdivision of projections by trace
\cite[III.1.7.9--10, p.~257; III.2.5.4(iii) and Theorem~III.2.5.7,
p.~279]{BlackadarOperatorAlgebras}.
For a finite von Neumann
algebra \((P,\tau)\), put
\(\norm{x}_2=\tau(x^*x)^{1/2}\) and
\(\norm{x}_1=\tau(|x|)\). Fix a free ultrafilter \(\omega\) on
\(\N\). The tracial ultrapower \(P^\omega\) is the quotient of the
bounded sequences in \(P\) by those with
\(\lim_{j\to\omega}\norm{x_j}_2=0\); its trace is
\(\tau_\omega((x_j)_\omega)=\lim_{j\to\omega}\tau(x_j)\).
We identify \(P\) with its constant sequences.

\begin{lemma}[Transfer from the trace to a normal representation]
\label{lem:trace-transfer}
Let \(P\subseteq\B(K)\) be a finite von Neumann algebra with faithful
normal trace \(\tau\).
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item If \((x_j)\) is bounded and
\(\lim_{j\to\omega}\norm{x_j}_2=0\), then
\(\lim_{j\to\omega}\norm{x_j\xi}=0\) for every \(\xi\in K\).
\item If \(x=(x_j)_\omega\in P^\omega\), then the weak-operator
ultralimit of \(x_j\) in this representation is \(E_P(x)\), where
\(E_P:P^\omega\to P\) is the trace-preserving conditional expectation.
\end{enumerate}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The functionals \(a\mapsto\tau(ba)\), \(b\in P\), are norm dense in
the predual \(P_*\). Indeed, their annihilator in
\((P_*)^*=P\) is zero, by faithfulness of the trace, so
Hahn--Banach gives the density.
For a normal vector functional \(\varphi\), approximate \(\varphi\)
in norm by one of these functionals. If \(\norm{x_j}\le K_0\), then
\[
 |\varphi(x_j^*x_j)|
 \le K_0^2\norm{\varphi-\tau(b\,\cdot)}
       +\norm{b}\norm{x_j}_2^2.
\]
This proves (i). For (ii), the defining identity of the conditional
expectation gives
\[
 \lim_{j\to\omega}\tau(bx_j)
 =\tau_\omega(bx)=\tau(bE_P(x))\qquad(b\in P).
\]
The same predual-density argument, using boundedness, extends the
identity to every normal functional.
\end{proof}

\section{Preparing infinite factors and comparing modular graphs}
\label{sec:modular-preparation}

We now pass from infinite factors to a common modular setting.  The input is
ordinary closeness on a separable Hilbert space.  After one small adjustment,
proper infiniteness makes that closeness completely bounded.  A fixed
hyperfinite tensor factor then supplies an irreducible finite subfactor in a
state centralizer.  Aligning its left and right actions gives a common cyclic
separating vector.  The main estimate of this section compares the two Tomita
graphs uniformly under rescaling.  In \Cref{sec:modular-alignment}, this
estimate will permit a small change of position after which the modular
group of one algebra preserves both algebras.

\subsection{A fixed tensor factor and common position}

\begin{lemma}[Amplification by common isometries]
\label{lem:common-infinite-amplification}
Let $M,N\subseteq\B(H)$ contain the same unital copy of $\B(\ell^2)$.
Then $\dcb(M,N)=d(M,N)$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
For each $n\geq1$ choose isometries $s_1,\ldots,s_n$ in that common copy
such that $s_i^*s_j=\delta_{ij}1$ and $\sum_i s_is_i^*=1$.
The operator $V:H^n\to H$ given by $V(\xi_i)=\sum_i s_i\xi_i$ is unitary.
For either $P=M$ or $P=N$,
\[
 V M_n(P)V^*=P,
 \qquad V[x_{ij}]V^*=\sum_{i,j}s_ix_{ij}s_j^*.
\]
Indeed the inverse coefficient formula is $x_{ij}=s_i^*xs_j$.
The same unitary therefore identifies the two amplified unit balls with the
two original unit balls.  Taking the supremum over $n$ proves the assertion.
\end{proof}

We fix, once and for all,
\[
 \lambda=e^{-1},\qquad \mu=e^{-\sqrt2}.
\]
For $0<\nu<1$, let $\rho_\nu$ be the state of $M_2(\C)$ with density
$(1+\nu)^{-1}\operatorname{diag}(1,\nu)$.  Form a countable infinite
tensor product containing infinitely many sites of each of the two types
$(M_2(\C),\rho_\lambda)$ and $(M_2(\C),\rho_\mu)$, and denote its von
Neumann algebra and product state by $(D,\rho)$.  We use the tensor product
of the site standard representations, on a separable Hilbert space $K$.
The product vector $\Omega_\rho$ is cyclic for both left and right local matrix actions,
and hence is cyclic and separating for $D$.  Thus $\rho$ is faithful and
normal.  Both $D$ and its standard commutant are hyperfinite: their finite
site matrix algebras increase strongly to them.

We recall the modular notation. In a standard representation with a
cyclic separating vector $\Omega$ implementing a faithful normal state
$\psi$, the closure of $x\Omega\mapsto x^*\Omega$ has polar
decomposition $S=J\Delta^{1/2}$. The antilinear isometry $J$ is the
modular conjugation, and $\sigma_t^\psi(x)=\Delta^{it}x\Delta^{-it}$
is the modular automorphism group. The state determines this action
independently of the chosen standard representation; see
\cite{Takesaki2003II} for Tomita--Takesaki theory.

For a faithful normal state $\psi$ on an algebra $P$, its
\emph{centralizer} is
\[
 P_\psi=\{a\in P:\psi(ax)=\psi(xa)\text{ for every }x\in P\}.
\]
It is also the fixed algebra of the modular automorphism group
$\sigma^\psi$.  We use the following precise continuous-core facts.  The
modular crossed product $P\rtimes_{\sigma^\psi}\R$ is semifinite,
with a faithful normal semifinite trace scaled by its
dual action \cite[III.4.8.1--4, p.~329]{BlackadarOperatorAlgebras}.
For a type $\III$ factor $P$, this crossed product is a factor exactly
when $P$ is of type $\III_1$; in that case it is of type $\II_\infty$
\cite[Lemma~8.2 and Corollary~9.7]{Takesaki1973}.
For a semifinite factor, choose a faithful normal semifinite trace $\tau$.
The modular crossed product is independent, up to isomorphism, of the
faithful normal semifinite weight used to form it
\cite[III.4.8.1, p.~329]{BlackadarOperatorAlgebras}.
Since $\sigma^\tau$ is trivial, this crossed product is
$P\barotimes L(\R)\cong P\barotimes L^\infty(\R)$ and is not a factor.
Here $L(\R)$ is the von Neumann algebra generated by translations on
$L^2(\R)$, identified with $L^\infty(\R)$ by Fourier transform.
Thus a factor has a factorial modular crossed product precisely when
it is of type $\III_1$.

\section{Uniformity and commutator estimates}
\label{app:comparison}

The proof distinguishes ordinary norm control, control at every matrix
size, and implementation on the original Hilbert space. We compare the
uniformity required for these steps with the commutator estimate in the
similarity companion, and then record how the small-unitary conclusion
controls both matrix gaps and commutants.

\subsection{Uniformity over factors and representations}

Fix an abstract type $\II_1$ factor $M$ with separable predual.
A stability statement uniform over its representations would assign,
for each $\eps>0$, a number $\delta_M(\eps)>0$ that works for every
faithful normal unital representation $\rho:M\to\B(H)$ and every
unital von Neumann algebra $N\subseteq\B(H)$: if
$d(\rho(M),N)<\delta_M(\eps)$, then a unitary within $\eps$ of the
identity conjugates $\rho(M)$ onto $N$. Even with this representation
uniformity, the tolerance may depend on $M$.

The quantifier order for universal stability is stronger:
the tolerance must be chosen before the factor as well as before its
representation. Positivity of each $\delta_M(\eps)$ does not imply
\[
 \inf_M\delta_M(\eps)>0.
\]
Consequently, a representation-transfer argument with absolute constants
preserves an already universal tolerance but does not by itself remove
factor dependence from its input.

In \Cref{thm:finite}, uniformity is obtained before the concluding
reductions. The common-position theorem has absolute constants, the
boundary argument in \Cref{prop:finite-standard-isomorphism} gives an
isomorphism with an absolute ordinary-norm bound, and
\Cref{thm:amplification} supplies an absolute amplification constant.
Their combination gives the single modulus $\eta_{\rm fin}$ for all
separably acting finite factors. Sections~\ref{sec:cores}
and~\ref{sec:reductions} propagate this uniform control through finite
corners, measurable assembly, and separable restrictions.

\subsection{Two commutator arguments}

The amplification theorem needed here concerns selfadjoint implementers
of commutators on separably acting type $\II_1$ factors. The similarity
companion proves a broader estimate: for every unital von Neumann algebra
$P\subseteq\B(K)$, every $Y\in\B(K)$, every integer $n\ge1$, and every
$X\in M_n(P)$,
\[
 \norm{[Y^{(n)},X]}
 \le C\norm{\ad_Y|_P}\norm X,
\]
where $Y^{(n)}$ is the diagonal amplification on $K^n$ and $C$ is
absolute, with no separability assumption
\cite[Theorem~1.2]{OpenAI2026Similarity}.

Both arguments use cyclic representation estimates and tracial free
products to obtain bounds independent of matrix size. In the present
paper, the column estimate of \Cref{lem:column-commutator} controls
randomized matrix coefficients. The free-word estimates bound their
commutators, while the averaged products converge weakly to a positive
scalar multiple of the identity in \eqref{eq:weak-scalar-limit}.
Together these facts yield \Cref{thm:amplification}.

The companion's central intermediate result is a corner estimate.
It works in a tracial free product $\mathcal L=D*A_0$, where $D$ is a
hyperfinite $\II_1$ factor generated by increasing full matrix algebras
and $A_0$ is a finite von Neumann algebra with a faithful normal tracial
state. Equip $\mathcal L$ with the free-product trace.
Writing $L_x$ for left multiplication by $x$ on $L^2(\mathcal L)$,
suppose that $G\in\B(L^2(\mathcal L))$ commutes with $L_D$ and that,
for some $e\ge0$,
\[
 \norm{[G,L_x]}\le e\norm x\qquad(x\in p\mathcal Lp),
\]
where $p\in D$ is a projection of trace $1/m$ for an integer $m\ge2$. For a
trace-zero selfadjoint unitary $s\in A_0$, the companion bounds the
compression of $[G,L_s]$ to $L^2(A_0)$ by $C_0e$, with $C_0$
independent of $m$ \cite[Theorem~3.1]{OpenAI2026Similarity}.
Its proof analyzes invariant tensors of reduced words, approximates
operators by right multipliers on small right supports, and obtains the
trace-independent bound from a Hankel compression
\cite[Sections~3--5]{OpenAI2026Similarity}. Using Popa's independence theorem,
the companion transfers this estimate to finite factors; passage through a
countable amplification treats their arbitrary separable normal
representations \cite[Section~6 and Proposition~7.1]{OpenAI2026Similarity}.

The finite stability proof here uses \Cref{thm:amplification} directly.
For the near-identity isomorphism $\theta:M\to N$ constructed there,
the switch operator on $H\oplus H$ has commutator with
$x\mapsto x\oplus\theta(x)$ whose off-diagonal entries are
$x-\theta(x)$ and its negative. Applying the amplification theorem to
this paired representation converts the ordinary bound on $\theta-\id$ into a
cb bound. \Cref{lem:paired} then supplies the unitary on the original
$H$. This identifies the precise role of commutator control in the
stability argument.

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Kadison's similarity problem asks whether the adjoint operation of a
\(C^*\)-algebra is respected, after a bounded change of Hilbert space
coordinates, by every bounded representation of its underlying algebra.
Kadison formulated the problem in 1955 in his study of the
orthogonalization of operator representations \citep{Kadison1955}.
Its force lies in the absence of any assumed relation between the
algebraic representation and the involution: multiplicativity and
boundedness alone must produce one equivalent Hilbert space inner
product for which all represented adjoints are correct.  This paper
resolves the problem positively in its unrestricted bounded unital form.

\begin{theorem}[Similarity]\label{thm:similarity}
Let \(A\) be any unital complex \(C^*\)-algebra, let \(H\) be any complex
Hilbert space, and let \(\pi:A\to\mathcal B(H)\) be a bounded,
complex-linear, unital algebra homomorphism.  There exists an operator
\(S\in\mathcal B(H)\), invertible with bounded inverse, such that
\[
  \rho(a)=S\pi(a)S^{-1}\qquad(a\in A)
\]
is a \(*\)-homomorphism.  In particular,
\(\rho(a^*)=\rho(a)^*\) for every \(a\in A\).
\end{theorem}

The theorem imposes no separability, nuclearity, finite generation,
faithfulness, or normality condition.  The similarity may depend on the
whole homomorphism.  The result concerns the existence of this single
bounded invertible operator, and does not require an a priori bound for
its condition number.

\subsection{Historical context}

The nuclear case was established by Bunce and Christensen
\citep{Bunce1981,Christensen1981}; see also the precise quantitative
comparison in \citet[Theorem~1]{Pisier2006Nuclear}.
Haagerup's theorem that every nuclear $C^*$-algebra is amenable
\citep[Theorem~3.1]{Haagerup1983Amenable} connects this case with the
cohomology of operator algebras. Complete boundedness provided the
principal analytic framework for the general similarity problem.
Haagerup solved the cyclic representation case and identified
complete boundedness as the criterion for similarity to a
\(*\)-representation \citep{Haagerup1983}. He also proved the similarity
property for $C^*$-algebras without tracial states
\citep[Proposition~1.8]{Haagerup1983}, and Christensen established it
for type~\(\mathrm{II}_1\) factors with property~\(\Gamma\)
\citep{Christensen1986}; see also
\citet[Section~1.2, Theorem~1.3]{Ozawa2006}. These cases explain the role
of the finite-factor argument below, where the estimate must be uniform
in the factor and its representation multiplicity.

Christensen established the
corresponding criterion for derivations: a derivation into the ambient
bounded operators is inner precisely when it is completely bounded
\citep{Christensen1977}.  Paulsen's similarity theorem extends the
homomorphism criterion to unital operator algebras and gives the optimal
condition number \citep[p.~226]{Paulsen1984}.  Kirchberg then proved that,
for each unital \(C^*\)-algebra, the similarity property is equivalent to
innerness of derivations in every faithful \(*\)-representation
\citep{Kirchberg1996}; we use the explicit per-algebra formulation in
\citet[Theorem~1.1]{Ozawa2006}.  Ringrose's automatic continuity theorem
allows this derivation property to be stated using bounded derivations
\citep{Ringrose1972}.

A von Neumann algebra is \emph{hyperreflexive} if the distance from
any operator to the algebra is bounded by a fixed multiple of the
supremum of its off-diagonal compression norms over the algebra's
invariant subspaces. More recently,
\citet[Theorem~2.4]{EleftherakisPaulsen2026} characterized a positive
answer to the similarity problem by preservation of hyperreflexivity
when adjoining a projection: whenever $M\subset\mathcal B(H)$ is
a hyperreflexive von Neumann algebra and $q\in\mathcal B(H)$ is a
projection, $W^*(M,q)$ is hyperreflexive. Their result is an
equivalence with this extension property and with the assertion that
every von Neumann algebra is hyperreflexive. Corollary~\ref{cor:hyperreflexivity}
below makes the latter consequence quantitative with one universal constant.

Pisier organized quantitative similarity estimates through the
similarity degree and its interpretation as the length of matrix
factorizations \citep{Pisier1999Degree,Pisier2001Remarks}.
His characterization of nuclearity by a similarity exponent below
three distinguishes the strength of the nuclear case
\citep[Theorem~1]{Pisier2006Nuclear}. These results concern quantitative
bounds for homomorphisms. The proof below is organized around a
uniform bound for derivations, and concludes with existence of a
similarity as stated in Theorem~\ref{thm:similarity}.

The companion result on discrete groups identifies unitarizability with
amenability~\cite[Theorem~1.1]{OpenAIUnitarizability2026}.
Unlike the homomorphisms in Theorem~\ref{thm:similarity}, a uniformly bounded
group representation need not have a bounded extension to the full or
reduced group $C^*$-algebra; the automatic extension is to $\ell^1(G)$.

\subsection{Cyclic domains}

The cyclic hypothesis needed below concerns only the domain
\(*\)-representation. The output representation may have arbitrary
multiplicity.

\begin{lemma}[Column factorization in a cyclic representation]
\label{lem:cyclic-factorization}
Let \(P\subset\mathcal B(K)\) be a unital von Neumann algebra with a
cyclic vector. For every integer \(h\ge1\) and every unit vector
\(\xi=(\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_h)\in K^h\), there are a unit vector
\(\zeta\in K\) and a contraction \(v=(v_i)\in M_{h,1}(P)\) such
that \(\xi_i=v_i\zeta\) for every \(i\).
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Put \(N=P'\), and choose a cyclic vector \(\Omega\) for \(P\).
It separates \(N\): if \(x\in N\) and \(x\Omega=0\), then
\(xa\Omega=ax\Omega=0\) for every \(a\in P\), whence \(x=0\).
Let \(L=\overline{N\Omega}\subset K\). This subspace reduces \(N\),
and restriction \(r:N\to\mathcal B(L)\) is faithful and normal.
Indeed, an element in its kernel annihilates \(\Omega\); normality
follows from compression to a reducing subspace. Thus it is a normal
\(*\)-isomorphism onto the von Neumann algebra \(r(N)\), and its
inverse is normal. The vector \(\Omega\) is cyclic and separating for
\(r(N)\).

The standard-form theorem for a representation with a cyclic separating
vector realizes every normal positive functional on \(r(N)\) as a
vector functional, with its vector in the natural cone
\citep[Lemma~2.10(1), pp.~278--279]{Haagerup1975}.
Apply it, through the normal isomorphism \(r\),
to
\[
 \omega(x)=\sum_{i=1}^h\langle x\xi_i,\xi_i\rangle,
 \qquad x\in N.
\]
We obtain \(\zeta\in L\subset K\) such that
\(\langle x\zeta,\zeta\rangle=\omega(x)\) for every \(x\in N\).
In particular \(\|\zeta\|^2=\omega(1)=1\). The assignment
\[
 x\zeta\longmapsto(x\xi_1,\ldots,x\xi_h),\qquad x\in N,
\]
is isometric, since both squared norms equal \(\omega(x^*x)\).
It extends to an isometry from \(\overline{N\zeta}\) into \(K^h\).
Extend it by zero on \(\overline{N\zeta}^{\perp}\), obtaining a
contraction \(v:K\to K^h\). The subspace \(\overline{N\zeta}\)
reduces \(N\), and the isometry intertwines the \(N\)-actions.
Therefore \(vx=x^{(h)}v\) for every \(x\in N\). Each coordinate
\(v_i\) lies in \(N'=P\), and \(v\zeta=\xi\), as required.
All these constructions, including the standard-form assertion, are
valid on nonseparable Hilbert spaces.
\end{proof}

\section{Introduction}\label{sec:introduction}

The Razak--Jacelon algebra \(\W\) is a simple, monotracial,
stably projectionless nuclear \(C^*\)-algebra
\cite{Jacelon}. Tensoring by \(\W\) removes the
\(K\)-theoretic part of the classification problem and makes the order
on the Cuntz semigroup visible through traces. The question is whether
the resulting trace data determine the algebra even when its ideal
structure is unrestricted. We prove that they do.

\subsection{The invariant and the main theorem}

For a \(C^*\)-algebra \(C\), let \(T(C)\) consist of all maps
\(\tau:C_+\to[0,\infty]\) satisfying
\[
 \tau(0)=0,\qquad
 \tau(a+b)=\tau(a)+\tau(b),\qquad
 \tau(ra)=r\tau(a)\quad(r>0),
\]
together with \(\tau(x^*x)=\tau(xx^*)\) and lower semicontinuity for
norm-convergent nets in \(C_+\). Arithmetic is extended nonnegative
arithmetic. We impose no density condition on the finite domain.
In particular, every closed two-sided ideal \(I\) contributes the weight
\begin{equation}\label{intro:ideal-weight}
 \tau_I(a)=
 \begin{cases}
  0,&a\in I_+,\\
  \infty,&a\in C_+\setminus I_+.
 \end{cases}
\end{equation}
The canonical topology is specified by
\begin{equation}\label{intro:trace-topology}
 \tau_i\longrightarrow\tau
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \limsup_i\tau_i((a-\eps)_+)
 \leq\tau(a)\leq\liminf_i\tau_i(a)
 \quad(a\in C_+,\ \eps>0).
\end{equation}
An isomorphism of these topological cones is a homeomorphism preserving
addition, the zero weight, and multiplication by every positive real
scalar.

\Needspace{3\baselineskip}
\begin{theorem}\label{thm:main}
Let \(A\) and \(B\) be separable nuclear complex \(C^*\)-algebras.
If \(T(A)\) and \(T(B)\) are isomorphic as topological cones, then
\[
 A\otimes\W\otimes\K\ \cong\ B\otimes\W\otimes\K,
\]
where \(\K=\K(\ell^2(\N))\) and all tensor products are spatial.
\end{theorem}

The conclusion is an actual \(C^*\)-algebra isomorphism.
The algebras may be nonunital, may have both finite and infinite
subquotients, and may have an arbitrary primitive ideal space.
Their only regularity assumptions are separability and nuclearity.
Moreover, the isomorphism can realize the prescribed cone map: after
transporting the given map to
\(F:T(B\otimes\W\otimes\K)\to T(A\otimes\W\otimes\K)\),
we obtain an isomorphism \(\Phi\) with
\(\tau\circ\Phi=F(\tau)\) for every extended trace \(\tau\).
This refinement is proved at the end of \Cref{pt:intertwining}.

The presence of \eqref{intro:ideal-weight} makes the invariant sensitive
to this ideal structure. For example,
\[
 I\subseteq J
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \tau_I+\tau_J=\tau_I.
\]
The finite and zero ideals of a general weight are also encoded by the
two limiting operations obtained by letting its positive scalar
multiple tend to zero and to infinity. These features will let us
localize each approximation on the ideal where its controlling trace
is finite.

\subsection{History and significance}

Razak's classification of simple inductive limits of stably
projectionless building blocks made the cone of traces, together with
its scale, an effective classification invariant
\cite[Theorems~1.1 and~2.1]{Razak}. Jacelon's construction singled out
the simple monotracial algebra $\W$ in this setting \cite{Jacelon}.
The existence, uniqueness, and approximate-intertwining organization
of those classification arguments also provides the broad method used
here, with new local estimates needed for arbitrary ideals.

The trace-cone question is due to Leonel Robert. It was recorded in
Santiago's 2012 conference abstract \cite{SantiagoWStable} and appears
as Problem~LXVIII in the survey of Schafhauser, Tikuisis, and White
\cite{STW}. Their formulation retains every extended trace, including
the zero/infinity ideal weights. Their May 2026 discussion describes
the known simple and traceless cases and the difficulty already
presented by one proper nonzero ideal. \Cref{thm:main} gives a positive
answer to that problem for the full cone and the unrestricted class of
separable nuclear algebras in its statement.

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

For a complex Hilbert space $H$, let $K(H)$ denote the $C^*$-algebra of
compact operators on $H$. Every nonzero irreducible representation of
$K(H)$ is unitarily equivalent to its defining representation.
Naimark's problem asks whether this property characterizes the algebras
$K(H)$. We give a negative answer in ZFC.

\begin{theorem}\label{na:main}
There exists a unital infinite-dimensional simple complex $C^*$-algebra
$A$ with a faithful tracial state such that all its nonzero irreducible
representations are unitarily equivalent. In particular, $A$ is not
isomorphic to $K(H)$ for any complex Hilbert space $H$.
\end{theorem}

Here a representation is irreducible if it is nonzero and has no
nontrivial closed invariant subspace. A tracial state $\tau$ is faithful if
$\tau(a^*a)>0$ whenever $a\ne0$. The last assertion of the theorem follows
from the first: $K(H)$ is unital only when $H$ is finite-dimensional.
All algebras and Hilbert spaces in the proof are complex, and no
separability assumption is placed on $A$.

Naimark's question dates to 1951; see the historical account of the
question and Rosenberg's affirmative work in \cite{AkemannWeaver2004}.
When the unique nonzero irreducible representation acts on a separable
Hilbert space, the algebra is isomorphic to the compact operators;
see \cite[Proposition~7.2]{CalderonFarah2022}. This condition concerns
an irreducible representation, not merely a faithful representation
on a separable Hilbert space.
Akemann and Weaver constructed a counterexample

counterexample from $\diamondsuit_{\mathrm{Cohen}}$ together with CH

counterexamples whose tracial state spaces are affinely homeomorphic

                                Dedicated to the memory of Shukoh Ishikawa


           Radial representations of finitely generated free groups are studied. The
           associated C*-algebra is located between the reduced and full group
           C*-algebras and its primitive ideal space is described concretely as a
           topological space.


                                               Introduction

    Spherical functions on finitely generated free groups have been investigated from
    various points of view. Among them, fundamental is the framework of Poisson
    boundaries, which allows us to take analogies with the case of semisimple Lie
    groups. In fact, studies of spherical functions go more or less around it and, as
    their basic properties, irreducibility and inequivalence of the associated spherical
    representations are established under this background.
       Other than spherical representations, a series of nonirreducible representations
    are associated with radial functions. Within that class interesting are positive
    definite functions of Haagerup, which include the standard trace as a limit case. For
    nonirreducible representations associated with positive definite radial functions, a
    generalization of Plancherel formula is described in [22] via spectral decomposition
    of radial functions based on the radial algebra which is commutative. Notice here
    that, different from the semisimple case, noncommutative free groups are not type I
    and the uniqueness of decomposition into irreducible representations breaks down.
       In other words, to obtain a Plancherel formula, we need to specify a maximal
    commutative subalgebra first and the above-mentioned Plancherel formula is based
    on the algebra of radial functions. As an instance, the standard trace belongs to the
    radial class and its Plancherel measure turns out to be the so-called Kesten measure,
    which is supported by the regular spectrum and equivalent to the Lebesgue measure.
       In this paper, we look into the primitive ideal space of radial representations and
    show that it is given by primitive ideals of spherical representations. Furthermore,
